title: Saudi Arabia vs the Houthis: Why the War in Yemen Started Again
author: Digest Editors
body:
Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, an armed group that controls much of Yemen, are fighting again. For four years things were mostly quiet between them. Now missiles, drones and air strikes are back. This is the picture as of early October 2026.

## Who are the Houthis?

The Houthis are a rebel group from northern Yemen. In 2014 they took over Yemen's capital, Sanaa. In 2015 Saudi Arabia and its partners started bombing them to bring back Yemen's old government. That war killed huge numbers of people and caused hunger across the country. Iran supports the Houthis with weapons and help, so many people see this as part of a bigger fight between Saudi Arabia and Iran.

In 2022 the United Nations helped both sides agree to a truce. The big fighting mostly stopped.

## How did it start again?

The calm started to break after the United States and Israel went to war with Iran in February 2026. In late March the Houthis joined in by firing missiles at Israel.

Then things turned against Saudi Arabia. On 13 July, Saudi Arabia bombed the runway at Sanaa airport to stop a plane from landing. A week later, on 20 July, the Houthis said they would block Saudi ships and Saudi oil in the Red Sea. They called it "an eye for an eye." On 25 July they attacked along the coast to take control of land next to the Bab al-Mandab, a narrow sea passage at the bottom of the Red Sea.

## What is happening now?

- In early September, Saudi officials said Houthi attacks on homes and energy sites had hurt at least 73 civilians, including women and children.
- On 19 September, Saudi Arabia said the Houthis tried to hit its capital, Riyadh, with a ballistic missile. It was the first attack aimed at Riyadh since the fighting started again.
- Both sides now say the other attacks them many times a day. There is heavy ground fighting around the Yemeni city of Taiz.
- In early October the Houthis targeted a Saudi oil facility.
- Saudi Arabia reportedly asked the United States for help. So far President Donald Trump has said no.

## Why does this matter to the world?

Oil. During the Iran war, Iran shut the Strait of Hormuz, the main exit for Gulf oil. So Saudi Arabia sent much more of its oil west, through the Red Sea. About 8% of the world's oil goes through the Bab al-Mandab. If the Houthis can block it, oil and shipping prices can jump everywhere.

## What could it lead to?

- **A long new war.** If neither side backs down, Yemen could slide back into the kind of war seen from 2015 to 2022, with more hunger for ordinary Yemenis.
- **Higher oil prices.** More attacks on ships or Saudi oil sites could push fuel prices up around the world.
- **A bigger regional war.** Saudi Arabia sees Iran behind the Houthis. If Saudi Arabia hits back at Iran, or the United States joins in, the Gulf could become a much bigger battlefield.
- **New talks.** Wars like this often end at the table. Oman and the UN have helped both sides talk before, and could try again.

Sources: Al Jazeera, NPR, CNN, ABC News (Australia), FDD.

title: America vs Russia: Peace Talks, Oil Deals and a Nuclear Warning
author: Digest Editors
body:
The United States and Russia are not at war with each other. But they are tied together by Russia's war in Ukraine, and right now they are talking and threatening at the same time. This is where things stand in early October 2026.

## The background

Russia launched a full invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. More than four and a half years later the war is still going. The United States has helped Ukraine with weapons and money. Since 2025, President Donald Trump has also tried to make a peace deal between the two sides.

## The talks

On 5 September, Russian President Vladimir Putin met two of Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, in Moscow. They then flew to Kyiv to meet Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Not much came out of it. Russia still wants Ukraine to give up land, and it points to its army's gains on the battlefield. Ukraine does not want to hand over its land.

There were a few small steps:

- Zelenskyy said Ukraine is ready for an "energy ceasefire". Ukraine would stop hitting Russian oil and power sites if Russia stops hitting Ukraine's power grid.
- Both Russia and Ukraine said they plan to restart three-way talks with the US, possibly hosted by the United Arab Emirates.
- The New York Times reported that Putin raised a big oil business deal with the Americans, as a way to show Russians they can do business with the US.

Meanwhile the fighting goes on. Russian strikes on Kyiv killed seven people in late September.

## The nuclear warning

On 30 September, Russia warned NATO that it was ready to use "the entire arsenal", including nuclear weapons, if NATO tried to cut off Kaliningrad.

Kaliningrad is a small piece of Russia on the Baltic Sea. It is not connected to the rest of Russia. It sits between Poland and Lithuania, which are both NATO members. Russia claims NATO is planning to block it by air and sea.

NATO's chief, Mark Rutte, said NATO is a defensive alliance and told Russia to "stop the nuclear threats". NATO says none of its exercises threaten Russian land.

Other tensions are building nearby. Poland raised its air defences after reports of aircraft entering its airspace. Denmark said a Russian warship fired flares near a Danish military helicopter over the Baltic Sea. A senior Russian diplomat said US–Russia relations are close to a major breakdown.

## What could it lead to?

- **A ceasefire, at least partly.** The energy truce idea is the most likely small win. It could stop attacks on power plants before winter.
- **A bigger peace deal.** This would probably mean hard choices about land, and safety promises for Ukraine. Neither side looks ready yet.
- **A dangerous accident.** With warships, jets and drones close together in the Baltic, one mistake could start a clash between Russia and a NATO country. That is the most serious risk.
- **More of the same.** Talks with little progress while the war grinds on has been the pattern for a long time, and it may continue.

Sources: Al Jazeera, The Moscow Times, US News / Reuters, House of Commons Library.

title: The 2026 Iran War Explained Simply
author: Digest Editors
body:
In 2026 the United States and Israel fought a short but huge war against Iran. Large-scale fighting has stopped, but the danger has not gone away. Here is what happened, in simple steps, as of early October 2026.

## How it started

For years, the US and Israel said Iran was getting close to being able to build a nuclear bomb. Iran said its nuclear work was peaceful. Iran also supports armed groups around the region, like Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen.

On 28 February 2026, the US and Israel attacked. They carried out nearly 900 strikes in the first 12 hours. They hit missiles, air defences, military bases and Iran's leaders. The US called it Operation Epic Fury.

## The biggest shock

Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in the first wave of strikes. He had ruled Iran since 1989. More than 40 top officials died too. A temporary leadership council took over until a new Supreme Leader is chosen.

Ordinary people paid a heavy price. A missile hit a girls' school next to a naval base in the town of Minab and killed about 170 people. Many Iranians had to leave their homes. They faced power and internet cuts and a stronger crackdown from the government.

## How Iran hit back

Iran fired hundreds of missiles and thousands of drones at Israel, at US bases and at nearby Gulf countries. It also closed the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea passage that carries a big share of the world's oil. Oil prices shot up.

The Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon also joined in against Israel.

## How it slowed down

The main US operation ended on 5 May. Pakistan helped both sides agree to a ceasefire, and in June they signed an agreement (an MOU) to stop the large-scale fighting. Since then, both sides have still traded some strikes, each blaming the other for breaking the deal.

The big questions are still not solved:

- What happens to Iran's nuclear program?
- Who controls shipping in the Strait of Hormuz?
- Will the US lift sanctions (trade punishments) on Iran?

## What is happening now?

In early October, President Trump warned Iran would be hit "very hard" if it was behind a co-pilot who tried to crash a flight to Israel. A third US aircraft carrier and thousands of troops are heading to the region, and Trump is weighing new strikes.

## What could it lead to?

- **A second round of war.** If the US strikes again, Iran could fire back at Gulf countries and shipping again.
- **A real peace deal.** A deal on nuclear limits in exchange for lifting sanctions is possible but hard, especially while Iran's leadership is still being rebuilt.
- **Change inside Iran.** Losing so many leaders at once is a huge shock. Iran could become more hardline, or more unstable.
- **Wars spreading next door.** The fighting has already reignited the war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen. More spill-over is possible.

Sources: Britannica, NPR, Al Jazeera, CFR Global Conflict Tracker, House of Commons Library, CNN.

title: Sudan's War: The Crisis the World Keeps Forgetting
author: Digest Editors
body:
While most headlines focus on the Middle East and Ukraine, one of the worst wars on Earth is happening in Sudan, in north-east Africa. This is where it stands in early October 2026.

## Who is fighting?

Two armed forces that used to work together:

- **The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF)**, the national army, led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan.
- **The Rapid Support Forces (RSF)**, a powerful paramilitary group led by General Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti.

## How it started

In 2019, protests pushed out Sudan's long-time ruler, Omar al-Bashir. The army and the RSF were supposed to help move the country to a civilian government. Instead, in 2021 they took power together. They then fell out over who would control the country and how the RSF would join the army. In April 2023 they went to war in the capital, Khartoum.

## What has happened since

The war has spread across the country. Millions of people have fled their homes, and the UN calls it one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with widespread hunger. Both sides have been accused of attacking civilians. The RSF has been accused of mass killings, especially in the Darfur region in the west. In late 2025 the RSF captured El Fasher, the army's last big city in Darfur.

## What is happening now?

- The RSF has stepped up deadly drone attacks on army-held towns in North Kordofan state, including the city of El Obeid.
- On 27 September an RSF drone hit a major fuel depot in Al Jazirah state.
- Fighting has grown sharply in Blue Nile state since August.
- The United States has proposed a 90-day ceasefire. An adviser to General Burhan criticised it, saying it could split Sudan into pieces, like Libya.
- A UN report in September found that foreign fighters and outside support are keeping the war going.

## What could it lead to?

- **Sudan splitting in two.** The army holds much of the east and centre, and the RSF holds much of the west. If the front lines freeze, the country could end up divided in practice.
- **More hunger and refugees.** Without a ceasefire and aid access, more people will starve or flee to neighbouring countries like Chad, Egypt and South Sudan.
- **A ceasefire.** The US 90-day plan is on the table. A pause could let aid in, even if a full peace deal takes much longer.
- **Pressure on outside backers.** If the countries sending weapons and money stop, the war could slow down. If they do not, it is likely to go on.

Sources: UN News, CFR Global Conflict Tracker, Security Council Report, Sudan Tribune, US News / Reuters.

title: Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab: Two Narrow Seas That Move the World's Oil
author: Digest Editors
body:
Two names keep coming up in this year's news: the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab. Both are narrow sea passages. When something goes wrong in either one, people around the world can feel it in the price of fuel. Here is why.

## What is a chokepoint?

A chokepoint is a narrow place that lots of traffic has to pass through, like a single bridge into a busy city. If you block it, everything backs up. The world's oil and goods travel mostly by ship, and a few narrow seas carry a huge share of that traffic.

## The Strait of Hormuz

The Strait of Hormuz sits between Iran to the north and Oman and the UAE to the south. It is the only sea way out of the Persian Gulf. Oil and gas from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE and Iran all pass through it. Roughly a fifth of all the oil the world uses goes through this one strait.

During the 2026 Iran war, Iran closed it. Oil prices jumped, and Gulf countries had to look for other routes.

## The Bab al-Mandab

The Bab al-Mandab is at the southern end of the Red Sea, between Yemen on one side and Djibouti and Eritrea on the other. Its name means "Gate of Tears". Ships use it to travel between Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal. About 8% of the world's oil passes through it.

Saudi Arabia has pipelines that carry oil across the country to Red Sea ports. When Hormuz closed, more Saudi oil went that way. That made the Bab al-Mandab even more important. It is also why the Houthis in Yemen fighting for the coast and threatening Saudi ships is so worrying.

## Why it matters to you

- **Fuel prices.** Less oil getting through means higher prices for petrol, flights and heating.
- **Shopping prices.** If ships have to sail the long way around Africa, it adds weeks and costs. Those costs end up in the price of goods.
- **Bigger wars.** Because these seas are so important, powerful countries send warships to protect them. That raises the risk of clashes.

## The simple takeaway

When you read that something happened near Hormuz or the Bab al-Mandab, it is not just local news. These two narrow seas are some of the most important pieces of water on the planet.

Sources: Al Jazeera, The Hill, Britannica, International Crisis Group.

title: The Transformer: The Idea Behind Today's AI Chatbots
author: Digest Editors
body:
Almost every big AI chatbot today is built on one idea from 2017: the Transformer. Here is what it is, in plain words.

## Where it came from

In June 2017, eight researchers at Google published a paper with a bold title: "Attention Is All You Need." It described a new way to build AI that works with language. They called it the Transformer.

## The old problem

Before this, AI read text one word at a time, in order, like reading with your finger under each word. That was slow, because each step had to wait for the one before. It also forgot things. By the end of a long sentence, it struggled to remember the start.

## The new idea: attention

The Transformer reads all the words at once. For each word, it asks: "Which other words matter to me?" This is called attention.

Take the sentence: "The dog chased the ball because it was fun." Attention helps the AI work out what "it" means by looking back at the other words, even if they are far away.

## Why it took off

Because it looks at all the words together, the Transformer works very well on modern computer chips, which are great at doing many things at the same time. So researchers could train much bigger AI on much more text, much faster.

It spread quickly:

- In 2018 Google used it to make BERT, which is good at understanding text.
- OpenAI used it to make the GPT models, which are good at writing text.
- Later it was used for pictures, sound, computer code and even proteins.

## Why it still matters

The paper became one of the most cited in computer science. Its big lesson was simple: a fairly simple idea, given lots of data and computing power, can beat more complicated designs. That lesson still shapes how AI is built today.

title: RAG: How AI Looks Things Up Before It Answers
author: Digest Editors
body:
AI chatbots learn from a huge pile of text, but that learning stops on a certain date. After that, they do not know anything new. They can also make up answers that sound right but are wrong. A method called RAG helps fix both problems.

## What RAG means

RAG stands for retrieval-augmented generation. That is a long name for a simple idea: look it up first, then answer.

## How it works

1. You ask a question.
2. The system searches a set of documents. These could be a company's help pages, a product manual or news articles.
3. It picks the parts that best match your question.
4. It gives those parts to the AI along with your question.
5. The AI writes an answer using that information.

It is like an open-book test instead of answering from memory.

## How it finds the right parts

Many systems turn text into lists of numbers that capture meaning. Text with a similar meaning gets similar numbers. So a question about "battery life" can match a paragraph about "how long the charge lasts", even though the words are different. Many systems also use normal keyword search to make results more accurate.

## Where it came from

The name comes from a 2020 paper by Patrick Lewis and his team at Facebook AI Research. Today the look-it-up-first idea is used in chatbots, work assistants and coding tools.

## Good points and limits

Good points:

- The AI can use private or brand-new information without being retrained.
- It can show you its sources, so you can check the answer.

Limits:

- If the search finds the wrong documents, the answer will still be poor.
- Long or conflicting documents can confuse it.

That is why good RAG systems spend a lot of effort on cleaning up and sorting their documents, not just on the AI itself.

title: The Fall of Constantinople, 1453
author: Digest Editors
body:
For over a thousand years, the city of Constantinople (today's Istanbul) was the capital of the Byzantine Empire, the eastern half of the old Roman Empire. In 1453 it fell. Here is the story in simple terms.

## The setting

By 1453 the Byzantine Empire had shrunk to little more than the city itself. All around it was the growing Ottoman Empire.

## The siege

In early April 1453, the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II, who was only 21, surrounded the city with a large army and a fleet of ships. Inside, Emperor Constantine XI had just a few thousand soldiers. They included fighters from Genoa in Italy, led by an experienced commander, Giovanni Giustiniani.

The city's best defence was its huge land walls, called the Theodosian Walls. They had stopped attackers for centuries. Mehmed brought something new: giant cannons. A Hungarian engineer named Orban helped build them. Day after day they fired heavy stone balls at the old walls.

## The ships over land

The defenders had stretched a big chain across the city's harbour, the Golden Horn, to keep enemy ships out. So Mehmed did something amazing. He had dozens of ships pulled over land on greased wooden tracks and put back into the water inside the harbour. Now the defenders had to guard even more of the city with very few men.

## The final attack

After weeks of cannon fire, the Ottomans attacked before dawn on 29 May 1453. Giustiniani was badly wounded and carried away, and the defence fell apart. Emperor Constantine XI died in the fighting. The city fell that same day.

## What changed

- Mehmed made Constantinople the new Ottoman capital.
- The great church of Hagia Sophia was turned into a mosque.
- The Byzantine Empire came to an end.
- The Ottomans became a major power in both Europe and Asia.

Many historians see 1453 as one of the moments when the Middle Ages gave way to the modern world. It also showed that cannons could now break even the strongest old walls.

title: The Cuban Missile Crisis: 13 Days Close to Nuclear War
author: Digest Editors
body:
In October 1962, the United States and the Soviet Union (today's Russia and its neighbours) came closer to nuclear war than ever before. It lasted thirteen days.

## How it started

On 14 October 1962, an American spy plane took photos over Cuba. They showed Soviet nuclear missiles being set up. Cuba is only about 145 km (90 miles) from Florida, so these missiles could hit much of the United States within minutes.

President John F. Kennedy saw the photos on 16 October. That is when the crisis began.

## The hard choice

Kennedy gathered a small team of top advisers. Some wanted to bomb the missile sites or invade Cuba. Others warned this could kill Soviet soldiers and start a much bigger war.

## The blockade

On 22 October, Kennedy told the country on TV about the missiles. He announced that US Navy ships would stop and check any ships carrying weapons to Cuba. He called it a "quarantine" instead of a blockade, because a blockade counts as an act of war. Soviet ships headed towards the line, and the world held its breath.

## The scariest day

27 October was the worst day. A US spy plane was shot down over Cuba and its pilot, Major Rudolf Anderson, was killed. Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev sent two different messages. The second one also asked the US to remove its own missiles from Turkey.

## How it ended

On 28 October, Khrushchev said the Soviet missiles would be taken out of Cuba.

- In public, the US promised not to invade Cuba.
- In secret, the US also agreed to remove its missiles from Turkey. This part stayed hidden for years.

## What came after

Both sides were shaken. In 1963 they set up a direct line between Washington and Moscow, called the hotline, so leaders could talk quickly in a crisis. They also signed a treaty banning nuclear tests in the air, in space and under water.

The lesson many people took from it: talking, even with enemies, can stop a disaster.

title: How This App Works Without Internet
author: Digest Editors
body:
This app works even when you have no internet. The trick is a browser feature called a service worker. Here is how it works, simply.

## What is a service worker?

It is a small piece of code that a website gives to your browser. It sits between the app and the internet, like a helper at the door. Every time the app asks for a file, the helper decides where to get it from.

## Saving files on your phone

The first time you open this app, the helper saves its main files on your phone: the page, the design, the code and the starter articles. After that, the app loads them straight from your phone. That is why it opens fast, even in airplane mode.

## Keeping things fresh

When you are online, the helper quietly checks for a newer version in the background. Next time you open the app, you get the update. This method is called stale-while-revalidate: show what you have now, and update for next time.

## Where your articles are kept

Articles you import are saved in a small database built into your browser, called IndexedDB. It can store hundreds of articles on your phone, ready to read and search offline.

## Tips for iPhone

Safari can clear saved data for websites you have not visited in a while. Apps added to the Home Screen are kept safer. So for the best offline reading:

1. Open this page in Safari.
2. Tap the Share button.
3. Tap Add to Home Screen.
